title: The Right Way to Sanction Russia
gist: Brooks and Harris argue Russia sanctions are not failing on their merits but on enforcement: the shadow fleet now carries two-thirds of Baltic tanker traffic, Russia's oil discount has vanished and its oil tax revenues ran $14 billion above year-ago levels from April to July, yet the fleet is structurally vulnerable because it buys aging ships from Greek owners, transits European waters and needs Western-dominated insurance.

insights.claim: One-fifth of Russia's GDP is directly linked to oil and gas extraction and exports account for nearly one-third of government revenues, making the oil trade the single highest-leverage point against Moscow's war financing.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Quantifies the transmission channel: a sustained cut to realized Russian export prices hits roughly a third of the federal budget.
insights.quote: One-fifth of Russia’s GDP is directly linked to oil and gas extraction, and exports account for nearly one-third of government revenues.
insights.locator: It is not too late to make sanctions effective

insights.claim: The closing of the Strait of Hormuz sent global oil prices soaring and handed Russia a massive windfall that is raising government tax revenue at a critical time, helping fund the Ukraine war and stabilize Russian financial markets.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Gulf supply disruption and Russian war-financing capacity are directly, positively correlated — a structural hedge relationship to model explicitly.
insights.locator: Russia continues to trade oil and other commodities

insights.claim: Russian oil tax revenues from April through July ran $14 billion higher than a year earlier, and by April the discount on Russian oil relative to global prices had all but vanished.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: The Urals discount is the cleanest single tracker of sanctions bite; its collapse to zero is the measure of current enforcement failure.
insights.quote: By April, the discount on Russian oil relative to global prices had all but vanished.
insights.locator: The Trump administration did sanction Russia’s two largest oil producers

insights.claim: Writing off sanctions as a wasted effort plays directly into Moscow's hands and discounts the strain properly enforced sanctions could still impose, because cutting hard-currency inflows could send the ruble into a depreciation spiral, drive inflation up and destabilize the broader economy.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Defines the intended mechanism — FX inflow to ruble to inflation — giving a monitorable chain rather than a vague policy hope.
insights.locator: But it is wrong to write off sanctions as a policy tool

themes.theme: How the price cap worked, then stopped working

insights.claim: Russia's current account surplus hit an all-time high of $235 billion in 2022 because the mere fear of a Western embargo drove prices up, letting Moscow nearly recoup its frozen foreign exchange reserves within a single year.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: The canonical case that supply-side sanctions on a major exporter can be self-defeating through the price channel — relevant to any Iran or Venezuela restriction.
insights.quote: Russia’s current account surplus, or the amount by which its export receipts exceeded its import payments, soared to an all-time high of $235 billion in 2022.
insights.locator: THE RISE OF THE SHADOW FLEET

insights.claim: The G-7's December 2022 price cap worked because around 70 percent of vessels shipping Russian oil were Western-owned and close to 90 percent used Western insurance, financing and brokering services, with the $60 crude cap set high enough to keep exports flowing but low enough to constrain revenue.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: The cap is a services-chokepoint design, not an embargo — its efficacy tracks Western share of shipping and insurance, which is the variable to monitor.
insights.locator: The solution the G-7 came up with in December 2022

insights.claim: By January 2023 Russian crude was selling for almost 40 percent less than the global benchmark, and Russia's current account surplus fell from $235 billion to $50 billion in 2023, recovering only slightly to $63 billion in 2024.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Demonstrates the cap can cut Russia's external surplus by nearly 80 percent when enforced — the upside case if Europe closes the gaps.
insights.locator: By January 2023, Russian crude was selling

insights.claim: Analysts warned that removing Russian oil — roughly one-tenth of global supply — from markets could lift crude from its prewar baseline of around $75 per barrel to $200 or higher and almost certainly drive the world into recession, which is why the cap was designed to preserve export volumes.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Sets the bound on how aggressive any Russia oil policy can be; volume-preserving measures are the only politically feasible ones.
insights.locator: Many oil and commodity analysts worried

insights.claim: The shadow fleet now constitutes around two-thirds of tanker traffic out of Russia's Baltic ports, which make up about half of Russia's seaborne oil exports.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Sizes the enforcement gap precisely — roughly a third of Russian seaborne exports move entirely outside the price cap regime.
insights.locator: As of today, the shadow fleet constitutes around two-thirds

insights.claim: By 2023 the shadow fleet was expanding by about seven oil tankers per month, with around half the ships purchased from Western owners, most of them based in Greece, and sales continued after the EU's December 2023 ban by routing through shell companies.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Greek shipowners are the named chokepoint; regulation targeting them is the most concrete near-term catalyst for shadow fleet attrition.
insights.locator: By 2023, the shadow fleet was expanding

insights.claim: Shadow fleet vessels are around five years older than the average operational tanker because owners want to minimize losses if the ships are sanctioned, which means the fleet requires frequent replacement to keep its numbers steady.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: The fleet's deliberate use of end-of-life tonnage is its structural weakness and creates a replacement-demand flow that can be interdicted.
insights.locator: It is now time to close those gaps

insights.claim: A U.S. sanctions listing is uniquely powerful because any entity doing business with a listed tanker risks exclusion from the dollar payment system, so the mere threat of secondary sanctions deters most companies — which is why 524 vessels sanctioned by the EU and Britain but not the United States continue shipping Russian oil unimpeded.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Isolates dollar-system access as the only sanctions instrument with real deterrent power; European listings without it are largely symbolic.
insights.quote: Without the threat of U.S. secondary sanctions, the 524 vessels that currently are subject to EU and British but not American sanctions have continued to ship Russian oil unimpeded.
insights.locator: Yet this success proved short-lived

insights.claim: The Trump administration sanctioned Lukoil and Rosneft in October 2025, driving down Russian oil prices, then undid that progress months later by granting multiple waivers to buyers as global prices rose during the Iran war.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Shows U.S. enforcement is procyclical with oil prices — expect sanctions relief precisely when prices spike, limiting their reliability as a policy anchor.
insights.locator: The Trump administration did sanction Russia’s two largest oil producers

insights.claim: The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act passed by the Senate in August will probably not make a significant difference, because its tariff authority is weak — the existing 25 percent U.S. tariff on India has not stopped India importing Russian oil — and the Trump administration has refused to use direct vessel sanctioning authority anyway.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Fade headlines about the Graham bill as a bearish catalyst for Russian oil flows; the operative variable is European enforcement.
insights.locator: TIGHTENING THE SCREWS

insights.claim: Europe holds decisive leverage over the shadow fleet because it passes through European-controlled waterways, replenishes its numbers with European-owned ships, and can be forced to engage with a Western-dominated insurance industry.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: The three-point chokepoint map for the trade: waterways, ship supply, insurance — each is a separate, actionable policy lever.
insights.locator: Russia evades Western oil sanctions primarily by using a shadow fleet

insights.claim: Brussels should extend its tanker sale prohibition to any transaction that ends in transfer to the shadow fleet through holding companies, and oblige European owners to sell only to jointly EU- and UK-approved buyers and to provide post-sale vessel tracking.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: A concrete regulatory change that would raise Russian fleet replacement costs — bullish for compliant tanker rates, bearish for secondhand sale values to opaque buyers.
insights.locator: It is now time to close those gaps, starting with the continued supply

insights.claim: Because international maritime treaties let states require vessels in their territorial waters to carry reputable insurance, pressuring flag states to enforce that rule would render many of Russia's aging tankers obsolete since they are insufficiently seaworthy to be covered — pushing the rest back into Western-dominated insurance and therefore under the price cap.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: The single most elegant enforcement mechanism proposed: insurance requirements convert Russia's use of old tonnage into a self-defeating strategy.
insights.locator: Europe has substantial economic power and a strong legal system

insights.claim: Interdiction is less escalatory than it sounds: Estonia, Finland, France, Germany and the United Kingdom have all stopped, inspected and occasionally seized shadow fleet vessels over the past two years without inviting any overt Russian retaliation.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Empirically caps the escalation risk premium on Baltic interdiction — the main argument European policymakers use against action has not held up.
insights.quote: these interdictions have yet to invite any overt retaliation by Russia
insights.locator: European countries would also have legal grounds to interdict

insights.claim: Refined product price caps are currently fixed dollar amounts well below market prices and should be switched to the 2025 crude model of 15 percent below trailing six-month market prices, which would auto-adjust after the Strait of Hormuz reopens without requiring every EU member state to approve each change.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: A formula-based cap removes the unanimity bottleneck — watch for it as the tell that EU sanctions are becoming operationally serious on refined products.
insights.locator: NO TIME LIKE THE PRESENT

insights.claim: These measures should not raise global energy prices because they preserve Russia's export volumes while shifting trade from the shadow fleet to legitimate tankers subject to European price caps, so EU policymakers have little to lose from implementing them.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: If correct, tighter enforcement is a Russia-revenue trade rather than an oil-price trade — an important distinction for how to express the view.
insights.locator: EU policymakers have little to lose

insights.claim: European appetite for bolder measures is growing amid U.S. inaction, Russia's increasingly effective sanctions evasion and rising concern that the war could spread beyond Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Robin Brooks
insights.so_what: Signals the political conditions for a step-change in EU enforcement are forming — a forward indicator for shipping, insurance and Urals spreads.
insights.locator: Until now, Europe has been reluctant to expand its sanctions
